body_html:
Talking to in-laws in Spanish is different from meeting them once. It is a long relationship built over visits, holidays, phone calls and the occasional awkward moment. Knowing the right vocabulary, how to address each person and a few phrases for everyday situations will help you feel part of the family rather than a polite guest. Here is what I wish every learner knew before their first year with Spanish-speaking in-laws.

Key takeaways
  • Learn the family words: suegro, suegra, cuñado, cuñada, concuño.
  • Ask how they would like to be addressed instead of guessing.
  • Phone and video calls are where your Spanish grows fastest.
  • Asking for advice and recipes builds closeness.
{{toc}}

In-law vocabulary in Spanish

SpanishEnglish
suegro / suegrafather-in-law / mother-in-law
suegrosparents-in-law
yerno / nuerason-in-law / daughter-in-law
cuñado / cuñadabrother-in-law / sister-in-law
concuño / concuña (Mexico), concuñadoyour spouse’s sibling’s spouse
consuegrosthe parents of your child’s spouse
la familia políticayour in-laws (the whole family)

Note that la familia política has nothing to do with politics: it simply means the family you joined by marriage.

How to address your in-laws

Customs vary widely. Some families expect señor and señora, or don and doña with a first name (don Carlos, doña Rosa), especially in rural areas and with older generations. Others prefer first names, or even mamá and papá after marriage. The simplest solution is to ask:

  • ¿Cómo prefiere que le llame? How would you like me to call you?
  • ¿Le puedo tutear? May I use tú with you?

Asking shows respect, and it saves months of uncertainty.

{{image:2}}

Talking to in-laws in Spanish during visits

  • ¿Cómo han estado? How have you been?
  • Los extrañábamos. We missed you.
  • ¿Les ayudo con las maletas? Can I help you with the suitcases?
  • Siéntanse como en su casa. Make yourselves at home.
  • ¿Qué se les antoja hacer hoy? What would you like to do today? (Mexico; also ¿Qué les gustaría hacer hoy?)

Phone and video calls

Calls can be harder than visits because there is no body language to help. These lines buy you time:

  • ¿Me escucha bien? Can you hear me well?
  • Se cortó un momento, ¿me lo repite? It cut out for a moment, could you repeat that?
  • Más despacio, por favor. Todavía estoy aprendiendo. More slowly, please. I’m still learning.
  • Le paso a [nombre]. I’ll pass you to [name].
{{book:a-road-in-bloom}}

Asking for advice and recipes

Few things warm a relationship like asking someone to share what they know.

  • ¿Me puede dar la receta de su mole? Could you give me your mole recipe?
  • ¿Qué me aconseja? What do you advise?
  • ¿Cómo lo hacía usted cuando sus hijos eran pequeños? How did you do it when your children were small?

Handling disagreements politely

Every family disagrees sometimes. Spanish has gentle ways to hold your ground without offense:

  • Entiendo su punto de vista, pero… I understand your point of view, but…
  • Lo vamos a pensar, gracias por el consejo. We’ll think about it, thanks for the advice.
  • Tiene razón en eso. You’re right about that.
  • Prefiero hablarlo con [pareja] primero. I’d rather talk it over with [partner] first.

More options are in {{link:disagreeing-politely-in-spanish|how to disagree politely in Spanish}}.

A sample phone call

  • Suegra: ¡Hola, mijo! ¿Cómo están? (Hi, dear! How are you both?)
  • You: ¡Hola, doña Rosa! Muy bien, ¿y ustedes? ¿Cómo sigue don Carlos de la espalda? (Hi, doña Rosa! Very well, and you? How is don Carlos’s back?)
  • Suegra: Mejor, por suerte. Oye, ¿vienen para Navidad? (Better, luckily. Listen, are you coming for Christmas?)
  • You: Queremos ir, pero todavía no sabemos las fechas. Le confirmamos esta semana. (We want to, but we don’t know the dates yet. We’ll confirm this week.)

Remembering a detail, like someone’s back pain, is the kind of thing in-laws notice and appreciate.

{{image:3}}

Holidays and special occasions

Holidays are when you will spend the most time with your in-laws, often surrounded by aunts, uncles and cousins. Some phrases for those days:

  • ¡Felices fiestas! Happy holidays!
  • ¡Feliz Año Nuevo! Les deseo mucha salud. Happy New Year! I wish you good health.
  • ¿En qué puedo ayudar para la cena? How can I help with dinner?
  • Gracias por incluirme en su familia. Thank you for including me in your family.

For birthdays, including your suegra’s, see {{link:birthday-wishes-in-spanish|birthday wishes in Spanish}}.

Building a real connection

Beyond politeness, a real bond grows from interest in their lives. Ask about their childhood, their town, their work, the old family photos on the wall: ¿Quién es este de la foto? (Who is this in the photo?). Share something about your own family too: Mi madre también cocina muy bien, pero nunca he probado algo así. Over time, these conversations become the relationship.

Common mistakes

  • Guessing the form of address. Ask once and you are set.
  • Translating “in-laws” literally. There is no en-leyes; use suegros or familia política.
  • Avoiding calls because your Spanish isn’t perfect. Short, regular calls build both the relationship and your language.

The RAE dictionary is useful when you meet a new family word. If this is your first visit, start with {{link:meeting-your-partners-family-in-spanish|meeting your partner’s family in Spanish}}, and for more situations see {{link:spanish-phrases-for-everyday-situations|my guide to Spanish phrases for everyday situations}}.

Final thoughts

A good relationship with your in-laws grows from small moments: a question about their day, a recipe you ask for, a call you make even when you feel unsure. Your effort to speak their language is a gift they will remember long after any grammar mistake.

faq.q: What is the Spanish word for in-laws?
faq.a: Suegros means parents-in-law, and la familia política refers to all the family you join through marriage.

faq.q: How do you say brother-in-law in Spanish?
faq.a: Cuñado is brother-in-law and cuñada is sister-in-law.

faq.q: Should I call my mother-in-law by her first name in Spanish?
faq.a: It depends on the family. Some prefer doña plus her first name, some señora, others her first name or even mamá. Ask her: ¿Cómo prefiere que le llame?
